Course overview

Short Stories and Visual Literacy

Use the Short Stories and Visual Literacy lessons and activities to build interpretation, evidence, and polished ELA 30-2 responses.

I can...

  • interpret how authors, playwrights, and filmmakers shape meaning.
  • select precise evidence and explain its analytical value.
  • develop sustained responses through the activity system for this unit.
  • deliberately collect useful work in a shared unit Evidence Bank.

Word structure or origin

Related terms

Short Stories - Introduction

In this unit you will have the opportunity to do the following:

  • Review the various elements of fiction and consider how they apply to the stories that you read
  • Compose a personal response to texts

Many short story texts provide questions at the end of a reading to help you deepen your understanding and appreciation of the story. One of the problems with these questions is that they are not your own.

  • You may be not ready to answer the questions that you are being asked
  • You may not agree with the line of questioning
  • You may feel that significant questions have not been addressed
  • You may limit your appreciation of a story by believing that the questions at the end of the story are the only important questions that need to be asked

Think about the following:

Learn to ask your own questions both while you are reading a story and after you have finished it.

Sometimes the questions you are left with will provoke you to go back and re-read a story to see if you can deepen your understanding.

What have you been learning about yourself as an independent learner? How will you be approaching your work in this next section of the course?

Lesson 1: Characters and Characterization

In narrative works or in a drama the persons who are presented are characters. In most pieces of fiction, one or two characters predominate and the action revolves around them. The central character in fiction is the protagonist and the major character or force that opposes the central character is the antagonist. Character refers to not only the fictional person but also their qualities. These qualities are an integral part of defining their character. A careful examination of a character's morals, disposition, and behaviour must be done in order to gain a full understanding of the character.

To determine the nature of a character, consider the following: How does the character behave?

What does the character choose to do or choose not to do?

What motivates the character?

What do others say about the character?

What does the character say?

Does the character change?

If the protagonist is essentially the same at the end of the story as at the beginning even though circumstances have changed, what aspect of the protagonist's character determined the direction of the protagonist's life? How does the protagonist deal with the antagonist? What internal conflicts, if any, does the protagonist experience?

Review

Before starting this lesson, you should watch this short video:

Classification of Character

A flat character is a minor character who is easily defined as they have only one quality.

A round character is a complex individual who has many evident qualities, therefore making them more difficult to define.

A stock character is an individual who is stereotyped.

A character foil is any character whose nature, actions or motivations serve to emphasize or highlight the nature, actions or motivation of another character.

A dynamic or developing character, often the protagonist, is one that undergoes and essential change throughout the fiction.

A static character, on the other hand, does not change in the course of the literature.

Characterization

The way in which an author reveals character is known as characterization. Two methods that are distinguished are Direct and Indirect Characterization.

DIRECT CHARACTERIZATION: The author explicitly tells the reader or has one of the characters tell the reader what a certain character is about.

INDIRECT CHARACTERIZATION: The author suggests what a character is like through what he thinks, says, does or does not do. This is usually the more convincing method of character presentation and challenges the reader to infer what a character is like.

Examples 

Types of Character

Example #1: The Lord of the Rings trilogy (By J. R. R.)

In The Lord of the Rings Trilogy, Frodo and his friend Sam discover their unexpected personal commitment, emotional and physical strength, and dedication to the cause. Gandalf discovers that his trust was broken by his fellow wizards, thus he transforms into a magician with a stronger character. Aragorn, an heir to line of kings, gives up his title; however, over the period of time he discovers his leadership skills, and decides to regain his crown. All of these characters provide us with good examples of round characters, each having depth of personality, and abilities to surprise the readers.

Example #2: A Christmas Carol (by Charles Dickens)

In Charles Dickens’ A Christmas Carol, Ebenezer Scrooge is a tightfisted person. He forces his workers to work hard, but gives them peanuts in return. However, after undergoing some very strange and disturbing experiences with the ghosts, he changes his ways – paying his employees more than their fair wages, giving them days off work, and even gives gifts. This transformation makes him fit into the role of a dynamic character.

Example #3: Hedda Gabler (by Henrik Ibsen)

Hedda Gabler is manipulative, cold, and “demonic,” even though she is the title character – the focus of the play. She is the most complex and psychologically compelling character, the reason that she is a dynamic character.

Example #4: Othello (by William Shakespeare)

At some points, it seems that Iago is the protagonist, since he dominates the entire play and delivers soliloquies. However, he does not change at all, and most of the protagonists undergo some sort of change during a play. Also, in the opening lines, Iago describes himself as someone who wishes to destroy Othello. Thus, his actions transform him into a tragic antagonistic type of character, though he is the central character of the play.

Lesson 2: Introduction to Elements of Fiction

As you read the following pages of explanations, as yourself, "Why is it important to learn literary terms?" There is, indeed, little point to simply memorizing definitions. Knowing terminology is of value only when you begin to apply your knowledge to help you make meaning of what you read.

As a student of ELA 30-2, you will be expected not only to understand the terminology involved with the study of the short story, but also to apply the knowledge to your reading and your explanations of what you have read.

Becoming comfortable with using these terms will help you communicate your ideas effectively and precisely.

Elements of Fiction Checklist

0/8 elements complete

DoneElementWhat to review
Types of Irony VERBAL IRONY occurs when a character says something that contradicts with what they have intended.
The point of view refers to the perspective from which the author chooses to present the narrative.
The plot is the sequence of events in the story.
When and where a story takes place is called the setting.
A symbol is something that means more than what it is.
Interpretive literature presents the reader with significant insights into life and into human nature.
"Diction" refers to the types of words the author uses.
The controlling idea or central insight of a piece of literature is its theme.

Irony

Types of Irony

VERBAL IRONY occurs when a character says something that contradicts with what they have intended.

SITUATIONAL IRONY occurs when both the character(s) and the audience are unaware of certain important information. There is a contrast between what is expected and what actually happens.

DRAMATIC IRONY occurs when the reader is aware of information that the character(s) are unaware of. What the character says or believes contrasts with what the reader knows to be true.

Irony involves a contrast between two elements. When irony is used, meanings tend to become concealed or contradictory.

Test Your Knowledge of Irony

  • Read the short story "A Little Cloud" by James Joyce. Identify the dramatic irony that is presented in the story.

Watch the video

Apply your understanding of irony

Choose an assigned short story. Identify a moment of verbal, situational, or dramatic irony, then explain how the contrast develops character, conflict, or theme.

Open the Text Bank

Lesson resources

  • Check your answer.
  • "A Little Cloud"

Point of View

The point of view refers to the perspective from which the author chooses to present the narrative. An author chooses the point of view that presents his/her story most effectively in terms of his/her purpose.

Identifying the point of view often increases the reader's understanding and interpretation of a story. The reader should consider why the author chose the point of view that is used. The point of view is the link between the author, the reader, and the characters.

Types of Point of View

First person point of view allows the author to disappear into one of the characters in the story. The narrator uses the pronoun "I". Whether the characer is the protagonist or an observer, their vantage point is "inside" the story.

Limited Omniscient point of view allows the author to tell the narrative through the eyes, mind and emotions of one character. It differs from first person point of view as the observations are told in the third person, "he" or "she".

Omniscient point of view or "all-knowing" allows the author to peer into the hearts and minds of several characters. He is able to interpret and comment on their behaviour, and even comment on the significance of the story.

Objective point of view does not allow for the thoughts of any of the characters to be revealed. The narrator refrains from making any observations. The story is told matter-of-factly-, void of any emotion.

Plot

The plot is the sequence of events in the story. It is the map that leads the reader through the story.

A short story must have conflict. The conflict may involve the central character, the protagonist, in an external conflict where s/he is pitted against one other person, a group of persons, or something outside of himself. The protagonist may also deal with internal conflict where s/he is at odds with his/her own emotions or thoughts. Often there is more than one conflict; however, there is generally one central conflict. The force that works against the protagonist is the antagonist.

The conventional plot has exposition, initial action, rising action, a climax, and falling action or denouement.

Elements of Fiction

Exposition: Exposition sets the time, place, mood or atmosphere under which the story occurs, introduces the characters and informs the reader of any antecedent action. This is usually given at the beginning of the story by the author. It serves as an introduction and gives the reader a chance to gain an impression of what has gone before and what is to come.

Initial Incident: This is the first event that sets the sequence of events, or the rising action, in motion. It need not be the first event in the story.

Rising Action: This is the interplay between characters and events that cause the problem. It is all the major events leading up to the climax.

Climax: The highest point of tension is the climax. It is the major crisis in the story and usually marks the turning point in the protagonists fortunes.

Falling Action/Denouement: The denouement follows the climax and constitutes part or all of the falling action.

Setting

When and where a story takes place is called the setting. While setting may have little effect in some stories, in many it significantly affects the plot, theme, and characters. Considering which aspects of setting are significant in determining the fate of the protagonist is frequently a clue to the underlying meaning of a story. If the time or place of the story changes, consider how those changes alter the outcome of the story.

The setting may suggest any or all of the following:

  • the prevailing atmosphere or mood of the literature

  • internal and external conflicts create potential contrasts between characters or ideas

Symbols and Motifs

A symbol is something that means more than what it is. It has a literal meaning but suggests or represents other meanings as well. Symbols are prevalent in our everyday life.

There are standard symbols that represent Canada and holidays (such as Christmas), as well as proofreading symbols that indicate changes that should be implemented before a final draft is produced. Symbols may also be represented graphically. We become so conditioned to standard symbols that we sometimes forget that they are indeed symbolic.

In literature, symbols add to and reinforce the meaning of a story, or they can, in fact, be the key to the story's meaning. When symbols or images recur throughout a piece of fiction they are called motifs. Tracing the pattern of a motif often offers meaningful clues to the theme of a piece of literature.

Although being on the alert for symbolic meaning is imperative, the reader must be cautious to recognize the following:

  • in order to be regarded as a symbol, it should be emphasized through repetition
  • a symbol's meaning needs to be consistent throughout the literature
  • a symbol may have more than one meaning

In literature there are many standard symbols. The following are some examples of symbols followed by their symbolic meanings:

  • an open window = freedom
  • white = purity
  • winter = death
  • bathing = purification
  • island = isolation
  • ocean = universal life
  • lamb = meekness

Tone and Mood

Interpretive literature presents the reader with significant insights into life and into human nature. Such truths take a greater hold when they are conveyed through our feelings as well as through our intellect.

Indentifying tone (the attitude of the author toward his audience and characters) and mood (the feeling a piece of literature arouses within the reader) is an important clue to help the reader discover literary themes.

Considering how a writer creates a certain tone and mood helps the reader appreciate the author's style.

Emotion producing insight, not emotion for its own sake, is the aim of interpretive reader.

Diction

"Diction" refers to the types of words the author uses. The writer's use of diction depends on subject, purpose, characters and style. In "Dr Heidegger's Experiment" Hawthorne uses a nineteenth-century style of diction that was appropriate for his time.

Points about diction:

  • words may be mainly monosyllabic (one syllable e. g. "help") or polysyllabic (more than one syllable e. g. "helpless")
  • words may be mainly colloquial or informal, archaic (language that was once used but is now out of date) etc.
  • words may be mainly denotative (to be interpreted literally) or connotative (suggesting figurative meanings)
  • words may be mainly abstract or concrete
  • words may be granting (unpleasant, harsh) or euphonious (pleasant, musical).

Theme

The controlling idea or central insight of a piece of literature is its theme. It is the underlying philosophical idea that the literature conveys.

Exploring themes increases our awareness of life, expands our horizons, and helps us feel truths about some aspect of life.

To determine the theme of a story, ask what insights into life or about human nature are revealed in the literature.

Literature that is written primarily to entertain gives theme little attention. The message presented can usually be reduced to a cliche. However, in interpretive literature, the focus is not on preaching a sermon but on making the reader think deeply, to offer a comment on life. Theme should not be reduced to a cliche but should provoke thought about human life and experience.

Themes often challenge our beliefs and provide somber truths:

  • They are derived from the literature but move to a generalized statement about human life. This comment may be stated in one sentence or explored in length, but it should encompass the entire selection. It should not be based on supposed facts or assumptions.

  • There is more than one way to state theme, and there may be more than one theme in a selection. However, there is usually one dominant impression that provides unity within the literature.

  • Because each reader is unique, a piece of literature may affect us differently. A reader need not accept a theme that is contrary to his or her personal beliefs; however, any theme is worthy of consideration in that it is someone's view. By sharing and refining many responses to the literature, we can move toward fuller interpretations and greater understanding of the theme.

Comparing Interpretations

Lesson 12: Literary Terms

As you read the following pages of explanations, as yourself, "Why is it important to learn literary terms?" There is, indeed, little point to simply memorizing definitions. Knowing terminology is of value only when you begin to apply your knowledge to help you make meaning of what you read.

As a student of ELA 30-2, you will be expected not only to understand the terminology involved with the study of the short story, but also to apply the knowledge to your reading and your explanations of what you have read.

Becoming comfortable with using these terms will help you communicate your ideas effectively and precisely.

Included on the link above is a list of literary terms that can help you interpret, critique, and respond to a variety of different written works. This list is by no means comprehensive, but instead offers a primer to the language frequently used by scholars and students researching literary works. This list and the terms included in it can help you begin to identify central concerns or elements in a work that might help facilitate your interpretation, argumentation, and analysis. We encourage you to read this list alongside the other guides to literary interpretation included on the OWL Website.

Literary Terms Reference

Purdue OWL Literary Terms

The Basics

Characterization
The ways individual characters are represented by the narrator or author of a text. This includes descriptions of the characters’ physical appearances, personalities, actions, interactions, and dialogue.
Dialogue
Spoken exchanges between characters in a dramatic or literary work, usually between two or more speakers.
Genre
A kind of literature. For instance, comedy, mystery, tragedy, satire, elegy, romance, and epic are all genres. Texts frequently draw elements from multiple genres to create dynamic narratives. Alastair Fowler uses the following elements to define genres: organizational features (chapters, acts, scenes, stanzas); length; mood (the Gothic novel tends to be moody and dark); style (a text can be high, low, or in-between depending on its audience); the reader’s role (readers of a mystery are expected to interpret evidence); and the author’s reason for writing (an epithalamion is a poem composed for marriage) (Mickics 132-3).
Imagery
A term used to describe an author’s use of vivid descriptions “that evoke sense-impressions by literal or figurative reference to perceptible or ‘concrete’ objects, scenes, actions, or states” (Baldick 121). Imagery can refer to the literal landscape or characters described in a narrative or the theoretical concepts an author employs.
Plot
The sequence of events that occur through a work to produce a coherent narrative or story.
Point of View
The perspective (visual, interpretive, bias, etc.) a text takes when presenting its plot and narrative. For instance, an author might write a narrative from a specific character’s point of view, which means that that character is our narrative and readers experience events through his or her eyes.
Style
Comprising an author’s diction, syntax, tone, characters, and other narrative techniques, “style” is used to describe the way an author uses language to convey his or her ideas and purpose in writing. An author’s style can also be associated to the genre or mode of writing the author adopts, such as in the case of a satire or elegy with would adopt a satirical or elegiac style of writing.
Symbol(ism)
An object or element incorporated into a narrative to represent another concept or concern. Broadly, representing one thing with another. Symbols typically recur throughout a narrative and offer critical, though often overlooked, information about events, characters, and the author’s primary concerns in telling the story.
Theme
According to Baldick, a theme may be defined as “a salient abstract idea that emerges from a literary work’s treatment of its subject-matter; or a topic recurring in a number or literary works” (Baldick 258). Themes in literature tend to differ depending on author, time period, genre, style, purpose, etc.
Tone
A way of communicating information (in writing, images, or sound) that conveys an attitude. Authors convey tone through a combination of word-choice, imagery, perspective, style, and subject matter. By adopting a specific tone, authors can help readers accurately interpret meaning in a text.
Types of narrative
The narrator is the voice telling the story or speaking to the audience. However, this voice can come from a variety of different perspectives, including:
First person
A story told from the perspective of one or several characters, each of whom typically uses the word “I.” This means that readers “see” or experience events in the story through the narrator’s eyes.
Second person
A narrative perspective that typically addresses that audience using “you.” This mode can help authors address readers and invest them in the story.
Third person
Describes a narrative told from the perspective of an outside figure who does not participate directly in the events of a story. This mode uses “he,” “she,” and “it” to describe events and characters.

Types of Prose Texts

Bildungsroman
This is typically a type of novel that depicts an individual’s coming-of-age through self-discovery and personal knowledge. Such stories often explore the protagonists’ psychological and moral development. Examples include Dickens’ Great Expectations and Joyce’s A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man.
Epistolary
A novel composed primarily of letters sent and received by its principal characters. This type of novel was particularly popular during the eighteenth century.
Essay
According to Baldick, “a short written composition in prose that discusses a subject or proposes an argument without claiming to be a complete or thorough exposition” (Baldick 87). A notable example of the essay form is Jonathan Swift’s “A Modest Proposal,” which uses satire to discuss eighteenth-century economic and social concerns in Ireland.
Novella
An intermediate-length (between a novel and a short story) fictional narrative.

Terms for Interpreting Authorial Voice

Apology
Often at the beginning or conclusion of a text, the term “apology” refers to an instance in which the author or narrator justifies his or her goals in producing the text.
Irony
Typically refers to saying one thing and meaning the opposite, often to shock audiences and emphasize the importance of the truth.
Satire
A style of writing that mocks, ridicules, or pokes fun at a person, belief, or group of people in order to challenge them. Often, texts employing satire use sarcasm, irony, or exaggeration to assert their perspective.
Stream of consciousness
A mode of writing in which the author traces his or her thoughts verbatim into the text. Typically, this style offers a representation of the author’s exact thoughts throughout the writing process and can be used to convey a variety of different emotions or as a form of pre-writing.

Terms for Interpreting Characters

Antagonist
A character in a text who the protagonist opposes. The antagonist is often (though not always) the villain of a story.
Anti-hero
A protagonist of a story who embodies none of the qualities typically assigned to traditional heroes and heroines. Not to be confused with the antagonist of a story, the anti-hero is a protagonist whose failings are typically used to humanize him or her and convey a message about the reality of human existence.
Archetype
“a resonant figure of mythic importance, whether a personality, place, or situation, found in diverse cultures and different historical periods” (Mickics 24). Archetypes differ from allegories because they tend to reference broader or commonplace (often termed “stock”) character types, plot points, and literary conventions. Paying attention to archetypes can help readers identify what an author may posit as “universal truths” about life, society, human interaction, etc. based on what other authors or participants in a culture may have said about them.
Epithet
According to Taafe, “An adjective, noun, or phase expressing some characteristic quality of a thing or person or a descriptive name applied to a person, as Richard the Lion-Hearted” (Taafe 58). An epithet usually indicates some notable quality about the individual with whom it addresses, but it can also be used ironically to emphasize qualities that individual might actually lack.
Personification
The artistic representation of a concept, quality, or idea in the form of a person. Personification can also refer to “a person who is considered a representative type of a particular quality or concept” (Taafe 120). Many classical deities are good examples of personifications. For instance, the Greek god Ares is a personification of war.
Protagonist
The primary character in a text, often positioned as “good” or the character with whom readers are expected to identify. Protagonists usually oppose an antagonist.

Terms for Interpreting Word Choice, Dialogue, and Speech

Alliteration
According to Baldick, “The repetition of the same sounds—usually initial consonants of words or of stressed syllabus—in any sequence of neighboring words” (Baldick 6). Alliteration is typically used to convey a specific tone or message.
Apostrophe
This figure of speech refers to an address to “a dead or absent person, or an abstraction or inanimate object” and is “usually employed for emotional emphasis, can become ridiculous [or humorous] when misapplied” (Baldick 17).
Diction
Word choice, or the specific language an author, narrator, or speaker uses to describe events and interact with other characters.

Terms for Interpreting Plot

Climax
The height of conflict and intrigue in a narrative. This is when events in the narrative and characters’ destinies are most unclear; the climax often appears as a decision the protagonist must make or a challenge he or she must overcome in order for the narrative to obtain resolution.
Denouement
The “falling action” of a narrative, when the climax and central conflicts are resolved and a resolution is found. In a play, this is typically the last act and in a novel it might include the final chapters.
Deus Ex Machina
According to Taafe, “Literally, in Latin, the ‘god from the machine’; a deity in Greek and Roman drama who was brought in by stage machinery to intervene in the action; hence, any character, event, or device suddenly introduced to resolve the conflict” (43).
Exposition
Usually located at the beginning of a text, this is a detailed discussion introducing characters, setting, background information, etc. readers might need to know in order to understand the text that follows. This section is particularly rich for analysis because it contains a lot of important information in a relatively small space.
Frame Narrative
a story that an author encloses around the central narrative in order to provide background information and context. This is typically referred to as a “story within a story” or a “tale within a tale.” Frame stories are usually located in a distinct place and time from the narratives they surround. Examples of stories with frame narratives include Canterbury Tales, Frankenstein, and Wuthering Heights.
In media res
Beginning in “the middle of things,” or when an author begins a text in the midst of action. This often functions as a way to both incorporate the reader directly into the narrative and secure his or her interest in the narrative that follows.

Terms for Interpreting Layers of Meaning

Allegory
A literary mode that attempts to convert abstract concepts, values, beliefs, or historical events into characters or other tangible elements in a narrative. Examples include, Gulliver’s Travels, The Faerie Queene, Pilgrim’s Progress, and Paradise Lost.
Allusion
When a text references, incorporates, or responds to an earlier piece (including literature, art, music, film, event, etc). T.S. Eliot’s The Waste Land (1922) offers an extensive example of allusion in literature. According to Baldick, “The technique of allusion is an economical means of calling upon the history or the literary tradition that author and reader are assumed to share” (7).
Hyperbole
exaggerated language, description, or speech that is not meant to be taken literally, but is used for emphasis. For instance, “I’ve been waiting here for ages” or “This bag weighs a ton.”
Metaphor
a figure of speech that refers to one thing by another in order to identify similarities between the two (and therefore define each in relation to one another).
Metonymy
a figure of speech that substitutes a quality, idea, or object associated with a certain thing for the thing itself. For instance, referring to a woman as “a skirt” or the sea as “the deep” are examples of metonymy. Using metonymy can not only evoke a specific tone (determined by the attribute being emphasized or the thing to which it refers), but also comments on the importance of the specific element that is doing the substituting. Note that metonymy differs subtly from synecdoche, which substitutes a part of something for the whole. For example, the phrase "all hands on deck" can substitute for the more awkward "all people on deck."
Parody
a narrative work or writing style that mocks or mimics another genre or work. Typically, parodies exaggerate and emphasize elements from the original work in order to ridicule, comment on, or criticize their message.
Simile
a figure of speech that compares two people, objects, elements, or concepts using “like” or “as.”
Previous Next Lesson

Lesson 11: Suggestions for Reading Short Stories

Read through the following steps to gain a better understanding of how to interpret short stories.

Step 1: Before you begin reading...

  • recall or research information on the author. Knowing the background of the writer and what themes or settings the writer often explores can help you interpret a story.

  • examine the title and consider possible meanings. The title is often a significant clue to help you identify the story's central ideas.

Step 2: As you read, interact with the story and try to identify...

  • the plot. How is it developing?
  • the characters. How does the plot develop the major and minor characters?
  • external and internal conflicts. How do they relate to one another?
  • the setting. What is its importance?
  • symbols and motifs. What ideas and images are being repeated in the story?
  • tone and mood. What feeling is the author trying to create in the story? Does it change? How does the author create the tone and mood?
  • theme. What are the central ideas of the story? Why did the author choose to end the story where s/he did?

Step 3: Reread the story or parts of the story to...

  • confirm your initial impressions
  • answer questions you have
  • alter or correct your ideas

Step 4: And lastly, concluding your reading...

  • use annotations and the study guide to record personal insights or reactions as a way of deepening your understanding.
  • continue to ask questions. The most important questions we are left with often do not have "right" answers.
  • examine the author's technique of writing and style. What traits dominate? How does the author's style contribute to the overall impressions of the piece?
  • rethink your ideas. Fit all the parts of the story into a whole by rereading and rethinking your ideas.

Lesson 13: Writing a Personal Response to Text(s)

The focus here is on the personal response.

This assignment is designed to:

  • Provide you with the opportunity to use a prose form of your choice to create a personal response that conveys your ideas as prompted by your reading of a text or texts (e.g. essay, short story, letter, article, script, monologue, dialogue, etc . . .)

  • Encourage the expression of your voice with an awareness of the intended audiences of the prose forms that you have chosenIntroduce you to the thematic topic of the analytical response.

What to expect?

Any combination of poetry, fiction, non-fiction, and visual texts as well as a brief comment relating the texts to a specific topic will be provided.

The question will give you the opportunity to write about what these texts suggest to you about the topic presented.

You are expected to select a prose form that is appropriate to the ideas you wish to express and that will enable you to communicate effectively to the reader. You will also be expected to support and develop your response with reference to one or more of the texts and your previous knowledge and/or experience. You may respond from a personal, critical, and/or creative perspective.

Suggestions for Writing the personal response

There is no prescribed answer or approach to the personal response. As you read and reflect upon the text, ask yourself the following questions:

  1. What ideas, feelings, or impressions does the text communicate to me about the topic?
  2. What have I experienced or learned that is relevant to my ideas, feelings, or impressions of the topic and/or the text?
  3. How might one or more of these texts relate to one another, my ideas, and the topic?
  4. What ideas and support will allow me to compose the most effective response to the topic?

When considering the prose form that would best communicate your ideas, ask yourself the following questions:

  1. What prose form will allow me to communicate my ideas and impressions most effectively?
  2. What prose forms have allowed me to communicate successfully in the past? Have I been able to maser a creative approach? Are my skills best suited to a formal or conventional composition?
  3. What prose form will best suit the ideas I wish to present?
  4. How can I use language and develop my ideas to make my writing communicate effectively?

Because students’ responses to the personal response vary widely—from philosophical discussions to personal narratives to creative approaches—you will be asked to briefly identify your choice of prose form, your reason(s) for choosing this prose form, and what you intend to communicate. As you indicate your choice of prose form, you may be directing your writing. Do not be afraid to change your approach as you think through your ideas.

Having confidence in writing about what a text (or series of texts) communicates to you will enhance the creation of your writing voice. Trust your ideas. Use your time efficiently. If your response is clear, focused, organized, on topic, and is supported by detail from a text(s) provided and from your previous knowledge and/or experience, you have done all you can to be successful.

ELA 30-2 | Literary Exploration Writing

Literary Exploration Guide

Use this six-stage sequence to explore an assigned idea through a provided text, a studied work, and a meaningful personal connection.

I can...

  • I can develop one controlling idea from an assigned prompt.
  • I can use an assigned text, a studied work, and a meaningful personal connection.
  • I can explain how each source of support develops the same idea.
  • I can revise for ideas, support, organization, language, and correctness.

Literary Exploration focus

A Literary Exploration develops one idea through three connected sources of support: the assigned or provided text, a studied work, and relevant personal knowledge or experience. Each section should deepen the same controlling idea.

Controlling Idea

A focused interpretation of the prompt that can guide the complete response.

Assigned or Provided Text

Precise evidence selected and explained from the text supplied with the prompt.

Studied Work

Relevant evidence from another work studied in the course.

Personal Connection

Knowledge, observation, or experience that deepens the exploration.

Presentation

Coherent organization, purposeful language, sentence control, and correctness.

Your writing path

Complete the six lessons in order. The final Preview combines the work saved in the active track exactly as entered.

  1. Prompt and Controlling Idea
  2. Introduction and Thesis
  3. Body 1 — Assigned or Provided Text
  4. Body 2 — Studied Work
  5. Body 3 — Personal Connection
  6. Conclusion and Revision
  7. Literary Exploration Preview

  3. Explain broader significance.
  4. Revise ideas, evidence, organization, language, and correctness.

ELA 30-2 | Personal Response Writing

Personal Response to Text Guide

Use this six-stage studio to connect a meaningful text idea to precise evidence and your own knowledge or experience in a purposeful prose form.

I can...

  • I can explore an idea, feeling, or impression prompted by the text.
  • I can use precise text evidence and relevant knowledge or experience.
  • I can choose a prose form and perspective that suit my purpose.
  • I can revise for development, voice, clarity, and correctness.

Personal response focus

A personal response asks you to explore an idea or impression from the text, support it with precise evidence, and connect it meaningfully to your own knowledge or experience in a purposeful prose form.

Idea or Impression

A focused response to the prompt that is worth exploring.

Text Support

Precise quotation, image, scene, action, or precise detail.

Knowledge or Experience

A relevant connection that deepens the meaning of the response.

Prose Form

A purposeful structure suited to the idea, audience, and effect.

Perspective and Voice

A personal, critical, creative, or blended approach.

Your writing path

Complete the six lessons in order. The final Preview combines the work saved in the active track exactly as entered.

  1. Prompt and Initial Impression
  2. Text Evidence
  3. Knowledge and Experience
  4. Prose Form and Perspective
  5. Shape the Response
  6. Draft and Revise
  7. Personal Response Preview
Course Lessons Next: Prompt and Initial Impression

ELA 30-2 | Personal Response Writing

God Is Not a Fish Inspector

W. D. Valgardson | Prompt and Initial Impression
Stage progress0 of 3 answered

I can...

  • I can identify what the prompt asks me to explore.
  • I can name a genuine reaction to the text.
  • I can turn that reaction into a focused idea.

Lesson

Separate the prompt from your first response, then turn that reaction into a focused controlling idea.

Model move

Begin with a genuine idea, feeling, question, or image from God Is Not a Fish Inspector, then shape that reaction into a focused direction.

Example

Identify one moment from God Is Not a Fish Inspector that stayed with you and explain the human question it raises for you.

Writing tip

Choose an impression that you can explore, not merely a like-or-dislike reaction.

How to apply it

  1. Restate the prompt in your own words.
  2. Name the moment or impression that stays with you.
  3. Explain why it matters to you.
  4. Shape the reaction into one controlling idea.

Prose Form and Perspective

Choose the form and perspective that best communicate your idea.

Responses save automatically

ELA 30-2 | Personal Response Writing

God Is Not a Fish Inspector

W. D. Valgardson | Prose Form and Perspective
Stage progress0 of 3 answered

I can...

  • I can choose a prose form that suits my purpose.
  • I can choose a clear perspective and voice.
  • I can identify the audience and effect I want.

Lesson

The response may be personal, critical, creative, or blended, but every choice must remain grounded in the text and prompt.

Model move

Choose the prose form, perspective, audience, and voice that make the controlling idea most effective.

Example

A letter, editorial, monologue, short essay, or blended response should sound and move differently because each form creates a different relationship with the reader.

Writing tip

Let purpose determine the form. Do not choose a creative form unless its structure strengthens the idea.

How to apply it

  1. Clarify your audience and purpose.
  2. Choose a prose form suited to that purpose.
  3. Select a perspective and voice.
  4. Plan how the form will shape the opening, development, and ending.

God Is Not a Fish Inspector

W. D. Valgardson | Draft and Revise
Stage progress0 of 3 answered

I can...

  • I can sustain my controlling idea through the full response.
  • I can integrate text support and personal knowledge purposefully.

Lesson

Use the plan as a foundation, then make the final response sound intentional and complete in its chosen form.

Model move

Use the plan as a foundation, draft the complete response, then revise for meaning, form, voice, clarity, and correctness.

Example

Read the complete draft once for the controlling idea, once for support and development, and once for sentence-level correctness.

Writing tip

Revise the larger meaning and structure before proofreading individual errors.

  1. Draft the complete response in the chosen form.
  2. Check that every section develops the controlling idea.
  3. Strengthen evidence, explanation, and connection.
  4. Revise voice, sentences, grammar, punctuation, and spelling.

ELA 30-2 | Visual Response Writing

Visual Response Guide

Use this six-stage sequence to move from careful observation, through PACES analysis, to a purposeful critical, creative, or personal response.

I can...

  • I can separate literal observation from supported inference.
  • I can analyze visual choices using PACES.
  • I can develop a controlling idea and intended unifying effect.
  • I can create and revise a purposeful critical, creative, or personal response.

Diploma connection

The ELA 30-2 Diploma Visual Response asks students to develop Ideas and Impressions and communicate them through effective Presentation. Current guidance suggests approximately 300–700 words; this written response is worth 10% of the Diploma Examination mark.

People or Subjects

Precise details about subjects, relationships, actions, expression, and gesture.

Angle and Composition

Viewpoint, framing, placement, focus, scale, and space.

Colour, Contrast, and Light

Visual choices that shape mood, emphasis, pattern, and attention.

Effect

The viewer response created by the combined visual choices.

Symbols and Suggestion

Supported interpretations that remain distinct from literal observation.

Your writing path

Complete the six lessons in order. The final Preview combines the work saved in the active track exactly as entered.

  1. Observe and Inventory
  2. Analyze Visual Choices using PACES
  3. Central Idea and Unifying Effect
  4. Choose a Prose Form and Plan
  5. Develop the Response
  6. Conclusion and Revision
  7. Visual Response Preview
Course Lessons Next: Observe and Inventory

ELA 30-2 | Visual Response Writing

Observe and Inventory

Record what is visibly present before deciding what the visual means.

Responses save automatically

ELA 30-2 | Visual Response Writing

Current Visual

Observe and Inventory
Stage progress0 of 5 answered

I can...

  • I can identify the visual and source when known.
  • I can separate literal observation from interpretation.
  • I can record precise details that may become evidence.

Lesson

Identify the visual and its context, record your first impression, and build a literal inventory without turning inference into fact.

Model move

Record what can be directly seen before deciding what those details might mean.

Example

Describe subjects, objects, setting, placement, gesture, visible text, colour, and light without presenting inference as fact.

Writing tip

Use language such as 'may suggest' when moving from observation to interpretation.

How to apply it

  1. Identify the visual and known source information.
  2. Record the first impression.
  3. Describe literal details.
  4. Build an evidence inventory.

ELA 30-2 | Visual Response Writing

Central Idea and Unifying Effect

Select the strongest details and form a defensible controlling idea.

Responses save automatically

ELA 30-2 | Visual Response Writing

Current Visual

Central Idea and Unifying Effect
Stage progress0 of 5 answered

I can...

  • I can select my strongest three details.
  • I can state a supported controlling idea.
  • I can acknowledge a reasonable alternative interpretation.

Lesson

Test more than one possible interpretation before choosing the idea and intended unifying effect for your response.

Model move

Select the strongest three details, test an alternative interpretation, and state one defensible controlling idea.

Example

Build the idea from a pattern across several details rather than from one isolated symbol.

Writing tip

Acknowledge ambiguity; a strong visual can support more than one reasonable interpretation.

How to apply it

  1. Rank the strongest details.
  2. Choose a precise keyword.
  3. Draft the controlling idea.
  4. Test an alternative interpretation and intended effect.

ELA 30-2 | Visual Response Writing

Choose a Prose Form and Plan
Stage progress0 of 5 answered

I can...

  • I can choose a form that suits my purpose.
  • I can keep critical, creative, and personal planning separate.
  • I can distinguish observation from creative invention.

Lesson

Select the branch that best serves the controlling idea. Clearly identify invented material when using a creative approach.

Model move

Choose the critical, creative, or personal branch that best serves the controlling idea and intended effect.

Example

A critical response proves an interpretation; a creative response invents a clearly identified situation; a personal response connects visual evidence to experience.

Writing tip

Keep separate plans so changing branches does not overwrite earlier thinking.

How to apply it

  1. Choose the response branch.
  2. Plan the branch-specific structure.
  3. Identify audience, purpose, and voice.
  4. Mark creative invention clearly.

  • I can develop the controlling idea using precise visual details.
  • I can sustain the intended voice and unifying effect.

Lesson

Use precise visual evidence and a deliberate prose form to create progression toward the intended unifying effect.

Model move

Build an opening and a sequence of movements that use precise visual details to develop the controlling idea.

Example

Move from one dominant detail to a contrasting or complicating detail before the final synthesis.

Writing tip

Create progression; do not repeat the same observation in different words.

How to apply it

  1. Draft the opening.
  2. Develop the first key detail.
  3. Extend or complicate the idea.
  4. Prepare the final movement.

Conclusion and Revision
Stage progress0 of 4 answered

I can...

  • I can complete the controlling idea in a form-appropriate ending.
  • I can assemble a coherent complete response.
  • I can revise for Ideas and Impressions and Presentation.

Lesson

Draft an ending that completes the unifying effect, assemble the response, and revise without erasing intentional voice.

Model move

Complete the response's unifying effect, assemble the full prose, and revise for Ideas and Impressions and Presentation.

Example

End with a realization, image, action, or synthesis that belongs to the selected form and follows from the visual evidence.

Writing tip

Revise meaning, support, form, and flow before proofreading correctness.

How to apply it

  1. Draft the final movement.
  2. Assemble the complete response.
  3. Revise ideas and visual support.
  4. Revise presentation and correctness.

ELA 30-2 | Short Stories and Visual Literacy

Writing Studio

Study literary terms in the assigned texts, keep useful evidence, and build a focused analytical paragraph.

Model bank

Analysis Explorer

Choose a literary term and a text. Supplied examples are clearly separated from your own analysis.

Character

Characterization

The methods a writer uses to reveal a character's traits, motives, relationships, and changes.
God Is Not a Fish InspectorW. D. Valgardson

Example 1

Textual or visual evidence

He wiped his forehead with his hand and cursed his infirmity.

Analytical breakdown

Fusi's private anger at his weakening body characterizes him as proud and fiercely independent; he treats age as an opponent rather than a condition he is ready to accept.

Plot

Conflict

A struggle between opposing needs, values, people, forces, or parts of a character's identity.
God Is Not a Fish InspectorW. D. Valgardson

Example 1

Textual or visual evidence

a quarter of a mile and one net were nearly beyond him

Analytical breakdown

The physical task exposes Fusi's internal conflict between the capable man he remembers and the limits his aging body now imposes.

Story World

Setting

The time, place, social conditions, and atmosphere in which a text unfolds.
God Is Not a Fish InspectorW. D. Valgardson

Example 1

Textual or visual evidence

no more than an hour and a half until dawn

Analytical breakdown

The dark shoreline and approaching dawn create a deadline. The setting turns Fusi's private trip into a race against exposure, pain, and time.

Narration

Point of View

The perspective through which information is selected, limited, and presented to the reader.
God Is Not a Fish InspectorW. D. Valgardson

Example 1

Textual or visual evidence

Now, he reflected bitterly

Analytical breakdown

The third-person limited point of view moves into Fusi's thoughts, allowing the reader to feel the bitterness that his daughter and neighbours may not see.

Layers of Meaning

Irony

A meaningful contrast between what is said, expected, intended, or understood and what is actually true or occurs.
God Is Not a Fish InspectorW. D. Valgardson

Example 1

Textual or visual evidence

Externally, he had changed very little over the years.

Analytical breakdown

The contrast is ironic because Fusi still looks strong while his unseen physical decline is steadily reducing what he can do.

Layers of Meaning

Symbolism

The use of a concrete object, image, place, or action to suggest meaning beyond its literal role.
God Is Not a Fish InspectorW. D. Valgardson

Example 1

Textual or visual evidence

the oars rising like too-small wings from a cumbersome body

Analytical breakdown

The wing image suggests freedom and power, but their smallness beside the cumbersome body makes the boat-and-oars image symbolize Fusi's diminished independence.

Language

Tone and Diction

Tone is the attitude created by a text; diction is the writer's deliberate choice of words that helps create it.
God Is Not a Fish InspectorW. D. Valgardson

Example 1

Textual or visual evidence

a bent shingle-nail twisted and turned in his shoulder socket

Analytical breakdown

The harsh verbs and jagged nail image create a punishing tone, making Fusi's pain feel mechanical, invasive, and impossible to ignore.

Central Ideas

Theme

A developed insight about people, choices, relationships, society, or experience that emerges across a text.
God Is Not a Fish InspectorW. D. Valgardson

Example 1

Textual or visual evidence

invisible deterioration that was gradually shrinking the limits of his endurance

Analytical breakdown

The story develops the idea that aging is frightening not only because the body changes, but because those changes threaten a person's identity and independence.

Character

The methods a writer uses to reveal a character's traits, motives, relationships, and changes.

half-gratefully, half-resentfully

The public party setting makes the mother's touching performative as well as private, increasing the son's embarrassment and revealing the social imbalance between them.

Point of View

The perspective through which information is selected, limited, and presented to the reader.

Example 1

Textual or visual evidence

her flesh has claimed possession of his

Analytical breakdown

The observing speaker interprets the mother's touch rather than merely reporting it, guiding readers to see affection and possession operating at the same time.

Irony

A meaningful contrast between what is said, expected, intended, or understood and what is actually true or occurs.

The flat claim is ironic after the smile has been linked with power and cruelty. It makes ordinary parental love seem capable of control as well as care.

The use of a concrete object, image, place, or action to suggest meaning beyond its literal role.

plays with the buttons on his shirt

The repeated use of the mother's hands symbolizes her continuing hold over her son, even as he approaches an age when he might pull away.

Language

Tone and Diction

Tone is the attitude created by a text; diction is the writer's deliberate choice of words that helps create it.

a loving smile, of course, but not altogether a friendly one

Analytical breakdown

The qualification 'but not altogether' shifts the tone from warm to uneasy, suggesting that love in this relationship contains pride, power, and threat.

Character

Textual or visual evidence

I need someone to love me the whole day through

Analytical breakdown

The direct admission characterizes the speaker as emotionally open and lonely, despite the freedom and experience he describes elsewhere.

Plot

Conflict

A struggle between opposing needs, values, people, forces, or parts of a character's identity.
Old ManNeil Young

Example 1

Textual or visual evidence

Love lost, such a cost

Analytical breakdown

The compressed line names the speaker's central emotional conflict: independence has not protected him from the pain and cost of lost connection.

Story World

Setting

The time, place, social conditions, and atmosphere in which a text unfolds.
Old ManNeil Young

Example 1

Textual or visual evidence

Run around the same old town

Analytical breakdown

The familiar town suggests repetition and emotional stagnation, contrasting with the speaker's claim that there is still 'so much more.'

Narration

Point of View

The perspective through which information is selected, limited, and presented to the reader.
Old ManNeil Young

Example 1

Textual or visual evidence

Old man, look at my life

Analytical breakdown

The first-person address makes the song a plea to be seen. The repeated 'my' keeps the listener inside the speaker's need for recognition.

Layers of Meaning

Irony

A meaningful contrast between what is said, expected, intended, or understood and what is actually true or occurs.
Old ManNeil Young

Example 1

Textual or visual evidence

Live alone in a paradise

Analytical breakdown

The contrast between 'paradise' and living alone complicates the idea of success: an ideal place cannot satisfy the speaker's need for companionship.

Layers of Meaning

Symbolism

The use of a concrete object, image, place, or action to suggest meaning beyond its literal role.
Old ManNeil Young

Example 1

Textual or visual evidence

Like a coin that won't get tossed / Rolling home to you.

Analytical breakdown

The coin suggests chance and instability; imagining one that will not be tossed expresses the speaker's desire for a dependable bond and a secure return.

Language

Tone and Diction

Tone is the attitude created by a text; diction is the writer's deliberate choice of words that helps create it.
Old ManNeil Young

Example 1

Textual or visual evidence

Old man, take a look at my life

Analytical breakdown

The repeated imperative 'look' creates an earnest, pleading tone. The speaker does not simply describe himself; he asks another person to witness him.

Theme

A developed insight about people, choices, relationships, society, or experience that emerges across a text.

Example 1

Textual or visual evidence

I'm a lot like you were.

Analytical breakdown

The refrain develops the idea that people at different ages share the same basic need for love, understanding, and a sense of belonging.

Point of View
